analysis.one_liner: Requires voting machine makers to disclose their software and bars conflicted labs from certifying voting systems.
analysis.headline: The electronic voting disclosure bill never left committee and drew zero cosponsors in two years.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added rules for the software inside electronic voting machines used in federal elections. Machine makers would have to give each state an updated copy of their voting software, let it be tested before every election, and disclose who wrote it and whether any of those people had been convicted of fraud. It would also bar testing laboratories with financial ties to voting machine makers from certifying voting systems, and require polling places to post notices telling voters how to file complaints about broken machines [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in federal elections. The bill would require voting machine makers to hand each state an updated copy of the software running their machines, require every type of machine to be tested for correct software operation before each election, bar labs with financial ties to manufacturers from certifying voting systems, and require public notice of complaint procedures when machines fail [S2][S3]. All of this aims to make machine elections verifiable and give individual voters a clear path to complain about equipment problems [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to give each state an updated copy of the software running their voting machines, making the code that counts votes available for state testing
Requires every type of voting machine to be tested to confirm its software works correctly no later than 30 days before a federal election and again on election day
Requires machine makers to tell the Election Assistance Commission who wrote the software, including whether any of those individuals has ever been convicted of a crime involving fraud
Bars the Election Assistance Commission from accrediting any testing laboratory that has a financial interest in voting system makers or is not sufficiently independent of them
Requires polling places to post notice that voters can file administrative complaints about broken voting machines or a jurisdiction's noncompliance

analysis.who_pays: Voting machine manufacturers would bear new costs and disclosure duties: handing states updated copies of the software that runs their machines, letting it be tested before each federal election, and reporting the identity and fraud-criminal-history of everyone who wrote the code [S3]. Accredited testing laboratories would have to prove financial independence from the manufacturers whose equipment they certify or lose their accreditation [S2][S3]. States and local election offices would face the logistics of pre-election machine testing and posting new public notices [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Voting machine makers and testing labs

drawbacks.text: The bill requires each voting machine type to be tested no later than 30 days before the election and again on election day, a deadline states and election offices with thousands of machines may have found difficult to meet

Requiring disclosure of every individual who wrote voting software, including fraud-related criminal history, raises privacy and staffing concerns for manufacturers without a clear limit on how that personal information would be used or protected

The bill adds a restriction of its own: an individual could no longer file a complaint about a broken voting machine unless they were eligible to vote on that machine, which narrows who can raise equipment problems to poll watchers and outside observers

The federal voting standards the bill amends were set up as voluntary guidance to states, and imposing new pre-election testing and disclosure conditions in time for the November 2006 election left a short runway

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real and the cost is borne mostly by the industry being regulated: verifiable software, independent testing, and a posted complaint process directly address known weaknesses in electronic voting, while manufacturers and labs absorb the compliance expense. The design has flaws — a tight pre-election testing deadline, personal disclosure of programmers, and a new limit on who can file complaints — but the complaint restriction exists to screen out frivolous filings and the rest is ordinary regulatory burden. On balance a modest, reasonable bill whose main cost fell on the companies it policed.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Administration committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the bill on February 1, 2005, amending the Help America Vote Act of 2002, which had created the standards and accreditation system for electronic voting machines
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration, the committee with jurisdiction over election administration
That referral was the last action ever taken on the bill; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded during the rest of the 109th Congress
Over its entire two-year life the bill attracted zero cosponsors, from either party
The Congress ended January 3, 2007, and the bill expired with it

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Voting machine manufacturers and the private testing laboratories that certify their equipment, who avoided new software-disclosure and conflict-of-interest rules for the rest of the decade. Voters gained nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Voting machine makers and testing labs

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to committee; the legislation then drew no further action and no cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bob Ney, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral the day it was introduced and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress

against.name: 0 cosponsors
against.what_they_did: No member of either party signed on during the two-year Congress, leaving the bill without a visible base of support

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so the issue never became a partisan fight; the outcome was decided by inaction rather than a vote.

industries.note: The bill would force makers to disclose the code running their machines to the states, submit to pre-election software testing, and identify every programmer and any fraud convictions among them. These rules cut against a business model built on proprietary, unauditable software.

industries.industry: Voting system testing and certification laboratories
industries.note: The bill would require the Election Assistance Commission to write standards preventing conflicts of interest, barring labs that hold financial interests in voting hardware or software makers from certifying systems. At the time, a small set of labs closely tied to the industry did most certification work.

States would gain clearer complaint channels and pre-election testing duties but would also bear the cost and logistics of testing every machine type before each federal election and posting public notices.
